newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Kuchma relishes Ukraine-NATO deal due in Madrid.
newsitem.headline: Kuchma relishes Ukraine-NATO deal due in Madrid.

text.p: IZMAIL, Ukraine, July 4 - President Leonid Kuchma, due to sign a special charter with NATO in Madrid on July 8 and 9, said the pact would give security guarantees to Ukraine and help plant the former Soviet republic's flag in Europe.
In an interview with Reuters late on Thursday at Ukraine's Danube port of Izmail, Kuchma also said the NATO deal would boost Kiev's strategy of integrating with European institutions.
"I am sure Ukraine's security will be increased," said Kuchma, in Izmail for a two-day summit with Emil Constantinescu of Romania and Moldovan President Petru Lucinschi.

"First, because this document consists of security guarantees. Second -- and this is one of the most important things -- it recognises us as a country of Central and Eastern Europe," he said. "In this way, we are invited into Europe".
The pact, initialled in May, is called the "Charter on a Distinctive Partnership between NATO and the Ukraine".

It sets up a series of mechanisms including an exchange of military missions, with NATO establishing an office in Kiev, ambassadorial meetings once a month and a bi-annual NATO-Ukraine Commission which will provide a vehicle for "consultations" at times of regional crises.
Kuchma sees it as a continuation of Ukraine's campaign to join Europe signalled last year when he said its strategic goal was to join the European Union.
In the last two months he has attended a string of regional summits in a bid to show Kiev's desire to boost ties with Europe and cut its umbilical cord to Russia.
Russia signed a Founding Act with NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, in May but Ukrainian officials see it as a "document with a spirit of confrontation".
They like to point out that Moscow is still opposed to NATO enlargement and see its document as a reconciliation of two opponents rather than a deal between friends.
Kiev, third in line for cash from Washington which has a strategic interest in strengthening its independence, stresses its NATO pact will be in a spirit of partnership.

Unlike Moscow, which dominated Ukraine for more than three centuries, Kiev does not oppose NATO enlargement and has recently shifted its position to open support for Central and Eastern European countries becoming members.
Ukraine was the first member of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) grouping former Soviet republics to join NATO's Partnership for Peace programme.
It has also boosted its profile in security structures by fulfilling a peacekeeping mission in Bosnia over the last five years, the last two years of it under NATO command.
Ukraine, although it is officially a member of the CIS, has never joined its Moscow-led Collective Security Pact, nor has its parliament ratified the CIS membership charter.

Ukrainian diplomacy has been anxious to get a formal deal with NATO and pressed for Kuchma to be invited to the Madrid summit, where he is due to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl.
Foreign ministry sources say the charter would not legally oblige the alliance to defend threatened Ukraine, a condition usually offered to fully-fledged members of NATO.
Kiev has not applied for membership of NATO but senior officials have suggested Ukraine might try to join after 2000.
Asked whether a time would come for Ukraine to abandon its official non-block status and neutrality to become a NATO member, Kuchma said: "There is nothing eternal in the world."
